subject: Post-demo: competitive TCO comparison and next tests

Subject: Post-demo: competitive TCO comparison and next tests

Hi Sara / Tom —

Thanks again for the demo time earlier. Quick recap + proposed next steps so we keep momentum:

Recap (what we covered)
- Primary goal: replace legacy transformer endpoints and reduce inference cost while improving 99th%-tile latency for your customer-facing assistants.
- Main concerns you raised: total monthly spend, tail latency, and ability to run private deployments for sensitive pipelines.

Where Redwood helps (differentiators we discussed)
- Unified runtime across hosted/dedicated/private so you can prototype on hosted and lift-and-shift to dedicated with no code changes.
- Cost controls: intelligent batching, KV/prefix caching, and quantization recommendations that materially reduce per-token spend.
- Reliability: automatic fallbacks and routing policies to keep SLAs during capacity events.

Initial TCO comparatives (back-of-envelope, attached spreadsheet has detailed assumptions)
- Redwood hosted (managed): ~$6 per 1M generate tokens (GPT-style dense models) under the demo config.
- Hyperscaler A (public): ~$12 per 1M generate tokens for comparable open models (per their published endpoint pricing).
- Hyperscaler B (other managed provider): ~$9 per 1M.
- Redwood Dedicated (reserved capacity, example 3-month commit): ~$1.8 per 1M (incentivized by reserved GPU pools + higher batching).

Key assumptions for the numbers above (see sheet): average 2k tokens per request, 30% cache hit, batching savings ~15% at batch sizes ~8, quantization equivalent quality tradeoffs for 8-bit.

Recommended next tests (to validate on your workload)
1) Short perf + cost run (48h): replay a /filtered/ production trace (100k–200k tokens/day) to capture latency and cost.
2) Cache experiment: enable prefix/KV cache for the FAQ flows and measure cache hit over 48h. Expect 20–40% hit for repeat queries; we’ll capture hit-rate/time.
3) Batching sweep: run same workload with batch sizes [1,4,8,16] to map latency vs cost curve.

What I need from you to kick off
- A non-production trace or representative prompt set (s3 link or sanitized CSV)
- Preferred 48h window (we have openings Wed/Thu next week)
- Any compliance constraints (SSO, IP restrictions) for the test environment

Attached: Redwood-TCO-1M-tokens.xlsx (detailed assumptions + per-1M cost math). Marcus will follow up with the exact test plan and formulas.

If this looks good, propose we schedule the 48h run Wed 2026-06-17 11:00am PT and I’ll create the POC workspace and invite your engineering contact.

From: Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwood.inference>

Hi Sara / Tom — Marcus (SE) here, quick technical follow-up and a worked example so the math is transparent. Attached are our lightweight benchmark logs from a recent 48h run (same model family).

How we measure cache hits
- We track cache hits at the prefix-key level (the key used for KV/prefix caching). Metrics emitted per request include: tokens_requested, tokens_served_from_cache, tokens_generated_from_model.
- Cache hit rate = tokens_served_from_cache / (tokens_served_from_cache + tokens_generated_from_model). We report both token-level and request-level hits.

Warm-up guidance
- For FAQ-style flows we typically see steady-state cache hit after ~12–24 hours of representative traffic. For bursty unique traffic it can be lower. For the 48h test we recommend a 6–12 hour warmup window and then a 36–42 hour measurement window.

Worked example (50M tokens / month baseline)
Assumptions:
- Base published cost (Redwood hosted) = $6 per 1M generated tokens (this is the unit we bill for model-generated tokens; cache-served tokens are not charged at model runtime).
- Average tokens/request = 2,000 (for your assistant flows).
- Cache hit rate = 30% token-level.
- Batching savings factor = 0.85 (i.e., effective model compute cost reduced by 15% at our observed batch sizes for this workload).

1) Raw generated tokens without cache = 50M
2) Effective generated tokens after cache = 50M * (1 - 0.30) = 35M generated tokens
3) Effective cost adjustment for batching = 0.85 -> modeled cost = 35M * 0.85 = 29.75M equivalent tokens (compute-adjusted)
4) Dollar cost = (29.75M / 1M) * $6 = $178.5 approx per month

Contrast (no cache, no batching)
- 50M / 1M * $6 = $300 per month

Contrast (hyperscaler published price $12 / 1M, same conditions)
- With 30% cache and batching 0.85: effective tokens = 29.75M -> cost = 29.75 * $12 = $357 per month

Dedicated reserved example (3mo commit)
- Unit cost example: ~$1.8 per 1M after reserved capacity and higher batching (we model batching factor ~0.75). With same 30% cache: effective compute tokens = 35M * 0.75 = 26.25M -> cost = 26.25 * $1.8 = ~$47.25 per month (note: this is illustrative; actual dedicated pricing is a function of reserved GPU count and utilization).

Notes + metrics we recommend capturing during the POC
- p50/p95/p99 latency (ms)
- tokens generated per second and throughput (tokens/sec)
- cache hit rate (token and request) over time
- cost per 1M and effective monthly spend projection
- GPU utilization / capacity headroom for Dedicated tests

I can spin up the POC workspace and pre-load the cache using a warmed prompt-set if you want to skip the warm-up window. Let me know which approach you prefer.

Regards,
Marcus Lin
